paragraphs: The paper studies how spoken dialogue models can learn from preferences in user conversations. Real-time speech involves more than choosing appropriate words: people interrupt, interject, and speak without clearly separated turns. These dynamics make preference-learning methods developed primarily for text difficult to apply directly to spoken interaction.

The researchers construct more than 150,000 preference pairs from raw conversations spanning multiple turns, using AI feedback to annotate them. The pairs cover variations in both linguistic content and temporal context. This gives the alignment process information about preferences concerning what is said and how speech fits into the unfolding conversation.

They use offline alignment methods to fine-tune a full-duplex, autoregressive speech-to-speech model—a model that can handle incoming and outgoing speech at the same time. Their experiments show that feedback from generic conversations can consistently improve factuality, safety, and alignment with conversational context. The reported benefits therefore extend across several aspects of response quality.

The team also deploys the fine-tuned model and conducts holistic human evaluations that examine interactions beyond individual turns. Their findings emphasize the importance of balancing conversational dynamics carefully. Improving natural spoken dialogue requires attention to how these dynamics work together across a conversation, alongside the quality of the language produced.
icml-2025-aligning-spoken-dialogue-model.tldr: AI-annotated preferences from speech conversations help fine-tune a spoken dialogue model for more factual, safer, and more contextually aligned interactions.

paragraphs: Determining whether one variable causes another becomes difficult when an unmeasured factor influences both. Earlier approaches use a proxy called a negative control outcome, or NCO, and test an integral equation. Their interpretation depends on an assumption connecting violation of that equation to the presence of a causal relationship.

The paper first develops a nonparametric procedure for situations where only an NCO is available. It retains asymptotic statistical properties while preserving more information than approaches that discretize continuous variables. The researchers also examine the underlying assumption itself: when the NCO affects the outcome, that assumption may fail, leaving the causal relationship unidentifiable.

They then consider settings with an additional proxy, a negative control exposure, or NCE. This extra variable supports another integral restriction that can discover causation when the NCO affects the outcome. Numerical studies support the proposed procedures and these findings. The contribution therefore combines a less restrictive statistical method with an explanation of when the original proxy-based reasoning can break down and how additional proxy information can help.
icml-2025-bivariate-causal-discovery-wit.tldr: A nonparametric proxy-based causal test preserves more information, while an additional proxy can address a specific identification failure.

paragraphs: Prompts sent to language model services can contain sensitive user information. Privacy protection must therefore balance how much it changes the input against whether the resulting prompt remains useful and efficient to process. Cape addresses this balance through a context-aware prompt perturbation mechanism based on differential privacy.

The mechanism introduces a hybrid utility function intended to capture token similarity more effectively. That similarity assessment guides perturbation toward alternatives that retain useful aspects of the prompt. Cape also uses bucketized sampling to manage a large space of possible selections. This component addresses the long-tail behavior that can arise when sampling from many candidates, making the selection process another central part of the design.

Experiments across multiple datasets, together with ablation studies, show a better privacy-utility trade-off than the prior state-of-the-art methods evaluated. The stated result concerns the balance between protecting information and preserving usefulness, rather than eliminating that trade-off. Cape's contribution is to improve this balance by considering both contextual similarity and how perturbation candidates are sampled.
icml-2025-cape-context-aware-prompt-pert.tldr: Cape combines context-aware token similarity and bucketized sampling to improve the privacy-utility trade-off in prompt perturbation.

paragraphs: A response that looks helpful on its own may do little to advance a user's larger goal. This paper argues that rewarding only the next turn encourages passive responses, especially when requests are ambiguous or open-ended. CollabLLM instead trains language models to account for how their responses contribute to an extended conversation.

Its central mechanism is a collaborative simulation that estimates a response's longer-term contribution. These estimates become multiturn-aware rewards for reinforcement fine-tuning. The intended behavior includes uncovering user intent and offering useful suggestions, so progress can involve helping clarify the task as well as answering the immediate request.

The researchers introduce a benchmark with three challenging interaction tasks, including document creation. Against their baselines, CollabLLM achieves average improvements of 18.5% in task performance and 46.3% in interactivity according to LLM judges. A separate user study involving 201 judges reports 17.6% higher satisfaction and 10.4% less user time. Together, these results support evaluating collaboration through both task outcomes and the experience of reaching them.
icml-2025-collabllm-from-passive-respond.tldr: CollabLLM rewards contributions across multiple conversation turns, improving task outcomes and user experience in its evaluations.

paragraphs: Combining information from different modalities requires representing how those sources relate to one another. In healthcare, for example, records, images, and notes provide different views of a case. This paper focuses on learning their joint distribution, arguing that common combination operations can oversimplify the interactions among their representations.

The proposed framework uses a copula, a statistical structure connecting the individual distributions of variables to their joint distribution. Here, the individual distributions describe the modalities, and the copula models their relationships. Treating this structure as an alignment mechanism gives the framework a way to capture complex interactions rather than relying only on concatenating representations or taking their Kronecker product.

The model assumes a Gaussian mixture distribution for each modality and a copula structure for their joint distribution. Under this design, it can also generate representations for missing modalities. Experiments on public MIMIC datasets report better performance than the competing methods evaluated. The findings support explicitly modeling cross-modal dependencies as a useful approach to both combining available information and representing an absent modality.
icml-2025-cross-modal-alignment-via-vari.tldr: A copula-based framework models relationships among modalities and can generate missing-modality representations under its distributional assumptions.

paragraphs: Label distribution learning represents an example using a distribution over labels, allowing several labels to describe it to different degrees. The paper identifies a tension in existing approaches: application-specific auxiliary tasks can provide useful guidance, but methods without such tasks may lack additional supervision beyond their main objective.

S-LDL addresses this by generating subtask label distributions. These distributions provide extra supervised information for learning the original label distribution. The subtask-generation algorithm does not require prior or expert knowledge, which is central to its intended generality. Rather than depending on an auxiliary task designed for one application, the method creates supplementary learning targets through its own procedure.

The framework is designed to plug into existing label distribution learning methods and can also adapt to derivative tasks. Analysis and experiments support its effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution is therefore both a way to construct additional supervision and a reusable framework for incorporating it. Its stated significance is that subtasks can guide distribution learning without requiring the application-specific auxiliary designs that motivated the work.
icml-2025-divide-and-conquer-learning-la.tldr: S-LDL generates subtask label distributions to give existing label distribution learners additional supervision without expert-designed auxiliary tasks.

paragraphs: An image detector can perform well on the generators represented in its training data yet struggle with images from an unseen generator. Gathering a large new synthetic dataset may also be expensive or infeasible, particularly for online generative models. This paper addresses both issues by making small amounts of additional data useful for detection.

The proposed Few-Shot Detector, or FSD, learns a specialized metric space for distinguishing AI-generated images. The central idea is to learn a representation in which very few samples can support detection of previously unseen fake images. The researchers also report that the method better captures common characteristics within categories of unseen images without requiring further training.

On GenImage, the experiments report a state-of-the-art result with an average accuracy improvement of 11.6% using only 10 additional samples. This finding supports the paper's emphasis on sample-efficient generalization across generators. The result is tied to the evaluated setting, while the broader methodological contribution is a learned comparison space that makes limited new examples more informative for image detection.
icml-2025-few-shot-learner-generalizes-a.tldr: FSD learns a metric space that supports detection of images from unseen generators using very few additional samples.

paragraphs: A subgraph's meaning can depend on its position within the larger graph, including relationships beyond its immediate neighborhood. Methods that emphasize local structure may overlook this information. However, aggregating too much global information can also blur the structural differences that make individual subgraphs distinguishable.

GPEN addresses these two concerns with complementary components. It uses a hierarchical tree to encode each node's global position through its path distance to the root. This provides a systematic representation of relationships involving distant nodes. A boundary-aware convolution module then selectively incorporates global structure while preserving the distinctive patterns within each subgraph.

The design matters because access to broader graph context and preservation of local identity are treated as separate requirements. Position encoding supplies distant structural information, while selective integration controls how that information affects the subgraph representation. Experiments on eight public datasets show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. These findings support the usefulness of incorporating global position without allowing broad aggregation to overwhelm the structure being represented.
icml-2025-gpen-global-position-encoding-.tldr: GPEN combines global position encoding with boundary-aware convolution to improve subgraph representations while preserving their distinctive structure.

paragraphs: Variable binding means associating a variable with its value, including when that value must be found by following other variables. The researchers train a Transformer on symbolic programs containing numerical assignments and variable-to-variable assignments. Queries require following chains up to four steps deep, while unrelated chains serve as distractors.

Analysis reveals three stages of learning. The model initially guesses numerical constants, then adopts a shallow strategy favoring early assignments, and finally develops a systematic way to follow assignment chains. This progression distinguishes successful dereferencing from an intermediate shortcut that can appear useful without implementing the full operation.

Using causal interventions, the researchers find that the residual stream serves as an addressable memory space. Specialized attention heads move information between token positions, allowing variable bindings to be tracked dynamically across layers. This mechanism supports accurate dereferencing in the studied programs. The finding provides a concrete example of a Transformer learning a symbolic operation without a built-in binding mechanism, connecting its internal computation to the program structure it must resolve.
icml-2025-how-do-transformers-learn-vari.tldr: A Transformer trained on symbolic programs learns to use its residual stream and attention heads to track variable bindings.

paragraphs: The paper asks which observed variables were directly targeted by an intervention on a biological system. It starts with paired observational and interventional datasets. This is challenging because biological data can contain thousands of variables but only tens of samples per intervention, and classical causal assumptions may not fit the system.

The proposed method first infers noisy causal graphs from the two datasets. A second component examines differences between those graphs, together with additional statistical features, and predicts the set of intervention targets. Both components are trained jointly under supervision using simulated and real data that reflect biological interventions. The graphs therefore provide structured evidence within a learned prediction system.

The approach consistently outperforms perturbation-modeling baselines across seven single-cell transcriptomics datasets. It also improves on current causal discovery methods when predicting soft and hard intervention targets across synthetic datasets. These findings support learning how changes in inferred relationships correspond to intervention targets. The method's practical focus is especially relevant when small sample sizes and biological complexity make direct application of causal discovery difficult.
icml-2025-identifying-biological-perturb.tldr: A jointly trained system uses differences between inferred causal graphs to predict which biological variables an intervention targeted.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a Transformer can carry out the training process of a deep neural network through in-context learning. Its contribution is a constructive positive example: the authors explicitly specify a Transformer that implicitly simulates gradient descent on another network using the information provided in context.

The construction uses a Transformer with (2N+4)L layers to simulate L gradient descent steps for an N-layer ReLU network. This formula connects the depth of the constructed Transformer to both the depth of the network being trained and the number of simulated updates. The authors provide guarantees for approximation within any specified error and for convergence of the in-context gradient descent procedure.

The analysis also extends to Transformers using Softmax, bringing the construction closer to that practical architecture. Experiments on synthetic datasets examine three-, four-, and six-layer neural networks, with in-context performance matching direct training. The findings establish that this form of deep learning through context is possible in the constructed setting; they do not assert that every trained Transformer automatically implements the same procedure.
icml-2025-in-context-deep-learning-via-t.tldr: An explicit Transformer construction can simulate gradient descent on deep ReLU networks through in-context learning, with approximation and convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper presents an exactly solvable example of in-context learning in a one-layer attention model. It interprets predictions as retrieval from associative memory conditioned on the examples in the context. This gives a concrete mathematical account of how those examples change what the model retrieves.

The account uses the modern Hopfield model, whose memory retrieval can be described through an energy landscape. Sequential examples in the context effectively reshape that landscape, changing the conditions under which retrieval occurs. Through the established equivalence between modern Hopfield models and Transformer attention, the authors connect this memory interpretation to the Bayesian model averaging view of in-context learning.

For Gaussian linear regression, the analysis characterizes how examples influence predictions and recovers a known epsilon-stability generalization bound for one-layer attention. The paper also offers explanations for three in-context learning behaviors and tests them experimentally. Its contribution is a bridge between memory retrieval and probabilistic interpretations within an analyzable setting, making the role of context mathematically explicit rather than merely describing it as additional input.
icml-2025-in-context-learning-as-conditi.tldr: An exactly solvable attention model interprets in-context learning as examples reshaping the retrieval landscape of associative memory.

paragraphs: Probabilistic forecasting must represent uncertainty as well as predict future values. The paper focuses on long horizons, where nonlinear dynamics can undermine accuracy and increase the computational cost of generative forecasting. It introduces K²VAE, a variational autoencoder-based model designed to address both difficulties.

The model combines two components with distinct roles. KoopmanNet transforms nonlinear time series into a linear dynamical system, giving subsequent prediction a simpler form to work with. KalmanNet then refines forecasts and models uncertainty within that linear system. Their combination is intended to reduce the accumulation of errors as predictions extend farther into the future.

Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art methods for both short- and long-term probabilistic forecasting, alongside improved efficiency. The approach matters because it connects the representation of dynamics directly to the forecasting procedure: transformation makes the dynamics linear, and refinement operates in that transformed system. The stated findings support this combination as a way to improve forecasting accuracy and computational efficiency while retaining uncertainty modeling.
icml-2025-k-2-vae-a-koopman-kalman-enhan.tldr: K²VAE combines a learned linear dynamics transformation with prediction refinement and uncertainty modeling to improve probabilistic forecasting.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced annotation often produces a sparse matrix because each worker labels only a few examples. Missing entries can weaken algorithms that combine worker responses into final labels. Earlier worker-similarity completion considers relationships among workers' labels on the same example, but overlooks information linking labels across similar examples.

LDPLC fills missing entries through label distributions. It first uses majority voting weighted by worker similarity to initialize a distribution for each missing label. It then repeatedly propagates neighboring label distributions, allowing each missing entry to absorb information associated with nearby examples. Once the distributions converge, the method uses them to assign the missing labels.

This process combines two sources of evidence: similarities between workers and relationships among examples. Keeping a distribution during propagation allows multiple label possibilities to participate before completion produces a label. Experiments on real and simulated crowdsourced datasets show that LDPLC significantly outperforms the earlier worker-similarity method in improving label integration. The reported benefit concerns the quality of the downstream integration process, which is the reason for completing the sparse annotations.
icml-2025-label-distribution-propagation.tldr: LDPLC completes missing crowdsourced labels by combining worker similarity with label-distribution propagation across neighboring examples.

paragraphs: Multimodal information bottleneck methods aim to keep information useful for a task while discarding unnecessary information from combined data sources. The paper identifies two obstacles: regularization weights are often chosen without theoretical guidance, and different modalities may contain unequal amounts of task-relevant information.

OMIB introduces an optimization objective for which an optimal multimodal information bottleneck is achievable when the regularization weight lies within a theoretically derived bound. It also adjusts regularization weights dynamically for individual modalities to account for unequal contributions and preserve all task-relevant information. These components connect the overall compression objective with the different informational roles of the input sources.

The authors provide an information-theoretic foundation and implement the framework using variational approximation for computational efficiency. Synthetic-data experiments validate its theoretical properties, while downstream evaluations report improvements over state-of-the-art benchmark methods. The theoretical claim is conditional on the specified weight bound and concerns achievability of the optimum. The empirical findings separately support the practical value of informed, modality-specific regularization when learning joint representations.
icml-2025-learning-optimal-multimodal-in.tldr: OMIB combines theoretically bounded regularization with modality-specific adjustments to preserve useful information in multimodal representations.

paragraphs: LotteryCodec explores whether an image can be represented through the structure selected inside a random neural network. Its lottery codec hypothesis states that untrained subnetworks can act as image synthesis networks with rate-distortion performance comparable to trained networks. Rate-distortion performance concerns the balance between compression size and reconstruction quality.

The encoder and decoder share an over-parameterized, randomly initialized network. For each image, the method fits a binary mask that selects a subnetwork, encoding image-specific statistics through that selection. The authors also introduce rewind modulation to help manage over-parameterization and streamline the search for an effective subnetwork. This mechanism improves the reported rate-distortion performance.

The paper reports that LotteryCodec outperforms VTM and establishes a new state of the art in single-image compression. It also allows decoding complexity to vary by adjusting mask ratios, offering flexibility for different device constraints. The central contribution is evidence that image-specific compression can rely on selecting structure within a shared random network, with the mask serving as the fitted representation.
icml-2025-lotterycodec-searching-the-imp.tldr: LotteryCodec compresses individual images by fitting binary masks that select useful subnetworks within a shared random network.

paragraphs: Class-incremental learning asks a model to learn new classes while retaining earlier ones, including when the task identity is unknown. Updating the model can move its feature representations, making old class knowledge harder to use. This study finds that differences in feature means and covariances primarily drive the distribution gap between new and existing tasks.

The proposed calibration method addresses both forms of movement. It represents each class mean by averaging sample embeddings, then estimates shifts using embedding changes weighted by proximity to the previous mean. For covariance, it applies a Mahalanobis distance constraint to align class-specific embedding covariances between the previous and current networks. These operations target changes in both where representations sit and how they are distributed.

The method also includes feature-level self-distillation to improve generalization. Experiments on commonly used datasets demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution is a concrete treatment of semantic drift through two statistical properties, connecting an observed source of representation mismatch to mechanisms designed to compensate for it as additional classes are learned.
icml-2025-navigating-semantic-drift-in-t.tldr: Mean-shift compensation and covariance calibration help preserve class representations as a model learns new classes without task identities.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes a structured geometry that can emerge in a trained network's final representations. This paper studies NC1, the property that representations within each class lose their variability. It analyzes a data-specific three-layer network whose first two layers operate in the mean-field regime, followed by a linear layer.

The main result links NC1 to the loss landscape. Points with both small empirical loss and small gradient norm approximately satisfy NC1, with the approximation controlled by those two quantities. This establishes a sufficient connection between fitting the training data, being close to stationary, and having tightly grouped within-class representations.

The authors also show that gradient flow on mean squared error converges to NC1 solutions with small empirical loss. For well-separated data distributions, they establish NC1 together with vanishing test loss. These conditions matter: the generalization result applies to certain distributions within the analyzed setting. The work connects representation geometry, training dynamics, and successful prediction through a common theoretical account, helping explain their observed co-occurrence.
icml-2025-neural-collapse-beyond-the-unc.tldr: In a mean-field network setting, small loss and gradient norm imply approximate NC1, with generalization results for well-separated data.

paragraphs: AUC is an important classification metric, particularly when classes are imbalanced. As learning methods increasingly optimize it, fairness across protected groups becomes a separate concern. This paper focuses on a practical complication: recorded group membership may be noisy, while existing AUC fairness methods often assume those labels are clean.

Incorrect group information can undermine the fairness a learning method is intended to preserve. The authors address this using distributionally robust optimization, developing a robust AUC fairness approach for noisy protected groups. They also provide theoretical fairness guarantees. The methodological emphasis is on accounting for unreliable group information within the optimization problem itself.

Experiments on both tabular and image datasets show better preservation of AUC fairness than the state-of-the-art methods evaluated. This evidence supports treating noise in protected-group labels as part of the fairness problem rather than relying on a clean-label assumption. The contribution is specific to fairness in AUC optimization: it combines a robustness-based formulation, theoretical guarantees, and empirical evaluation across two types of data.
icml-2025-preserving-auc-fairness-in-lea.tldr: A distributionally robust optimization approach preserves AUC fairness when protected-group labels are noisy.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer potential energy benefits, but long-term prediction poses challenges for encoding extended sequences. The paper also identifies a problem for spiking Transformers: inadequate positional encoding can limit how effectively their self-attention uses sequence position. SpikF addresses these issues with an attention-free forecasting architecture.

The model encodes input sequences in patches and uses a frequency-domain selection mechanism to exploit the sequential properties of time-series data. These choices connect the representation of long inputs with the way the model processes temporal information. The approach avoids relying on spiking self-attention, whose positional-information difficulties are one motivation for the design.

Across eight established long-term prediction datasets, SpikF achieves an average 1.9% reduction in mean absolute error compared with state-of-the-art models. The paper also reports a 3.16-fold reduction in total energy consumption. Together, these findings support the possibility of improving forecasting accuracy and energy efficiency at the same time in the evaluated setting, using patch encoding and frequency-based processing within a spiking network.
icml-2025-spikf-spiking-fourier-network-.tldr: SpikF uses patch encoding and frequency-domain selection for attention-free spiking forecasts, improving reported accuracy and energy efficiency.

paragraphs: Visual tokens can make large multimodal models computationally expensive. This paper investigates redundancy in the operations applied to those tokens. Its central observation is that representations produced by a pretrained vision encoder do not necessarily need every heavy self-attention and feed-forward operation in a decoder-only multimodal model.

The researchers use a series of experiments to identify and progressively reduce this computation. Their resulting method, ProxyV, introduces proxy vision tokens that alleviate the processing burden on the original visual tokens. The design aims to preserve visual information while changing how much computation is devoted to processing it.

The paper reports efficiency improvements without reduced performance, and notable performance gains in configurations with more moderate efficiency improvements. ProxyV can also be combined with token-reduction methods for further savings. This compatibility matters because reducing the number of tokens and reducing the work performed on tokens address different sources of cost. The findings support computation allocation as another useful design choice for making multimodal models more efficient.
icml-2025-streamline-without-sacrifice-s.tldr: ProxyV uses proxy vision tokens to reduce redundant visual computation while maintaining performance in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to train existing language models to generate explicit thoughts before answering general instructions. The objective extends beyond tasks conventionally labeled as reasoning problems. The method uses no additional human data and does not require direct supervision specifying what the thought process should contain.

Training alternates between searching for candidate thought generations and optimizing the model. For each instruction, a judge model evaluates the resulting responses only. Those response evaluations score the thought candidates, which then guide preference optimization. The learning signal therefore comes from the quality of the final answer rather than direct judgments of the intermediate thought text.

The researchers report superior performance on AlpacaEval and Arena-Hard. They also find gains in marketing, health, and general knowledge, alongside reasoning and problem-solving tasks. These results support the usefulness of learned thought generation across several instruction categories in the evaluated setting. The contribution is a training procedure that searches for helpful intermediate generation and reinforces it through answer-level feedback.
icml-2025-thinking-llms-general-instruct.tldr: Iterative search and preference optimization teach language models useful thought generation using feedback on final responses without additional human data.

paragraphs: Generating sequences as long as 100,000 tokens can take substantial time. This paper finds that simply extending the generation limits of traditional speculative decoding methods does not solve the problem and can make performance worse. It examines the obstacles that become important at these unusually long output lengths.

The analysis identifies three major challenges: repeated model reloading, dynamic management of key-value memory, and repetitive generation. TokenSwift is introduced as a framework for addressing these issues while maintaining the target model's inherent quality. The focus is therefore on making the generation process more efficient at long lengths without sacrificing the quality associated with the target model.

Experiments report speedups exceeding threefold across models with 1.5, 7, 8, and 14 billion parameters, including MHA and GQA architectures. The authors state that these improvements translate into hours saved for ultra-long generation. The breadth of the tested model sizes and architectures supports the framework's scalability within those evaluations, while the analysis explains why short-generation acceleration methods cannot simply be extended unchanged.
icml-2025-tokenswift-lossless-accelerati.tldr: TokenSwift addresses bottlenecks in ultra-long generation and reports over threefold speedups while preserving target-model quality.

paragraphs: This paper asks when language models actually help classify nodes in graphs. Its goal is to turn scattered performance results into practical design guidance through a systematic comparison. The researchers build LLMNodeBed, a shared codebase and testbed covering different graph structures, algorithms, and learning settings.

The testbed includes 10 homophilic datasets, four heterophilic datasets, eight LLM-based algorithms, eight classical baselines, and three learning paradigms. Across more than 2,700 trained and evaluated models, the study examines factors such as homophily, learning paradigm, model size, and prompting. This range allows the comparison to examine settings and components rather than treating LLM-based node classification as one uniform approach.

Among eight reported insights, LLM methods can substantially outperform traditional methods with semi-supervised learning, while their advantage is marginal in the supervised setting. In zero-shot evaluation, graph foundation models can outperform open-source LLMs but remain behind strong LLMs such as GPT-4o. These findings make the benefit conditional on the setting and model choice, providing more specific guidance than an overall claim that LLMs improve graph prediction.
icml-2025-when-do-llms-help-with-node-cl.tldr: A large node-classification comparison shows that LLM benefits depend strongly on the learning setting and model choice.

paragraphs: APT is a Transformer for zero-shot meta-learning on tabular prediction tasks that uses no real-world datasets during pretraining. Building on Prior-Data Fitted Networks and TabPFN, it learns from synthetic data. Its distinctive feature is that adversarial data agents continually change their generating distributions to present challenging datasets.

The framework also introduces a mixture block architecture that can handle classification with arbitrary numbers of classes. This addresses the class-count restriction of earlier tabular zero-shot methods. The paper's analysis finds that adversarial agents generate more diverse data than TabPFN's ordinary random generator, while the mixture block design improves generalizability and substantially accelerates pretraining.

On small tabular classification tasks, APT matches state-of-the-art performance with an average runtime below one second, without filtering datasets by characteristics such as class count or missing values. Adversarial pretraining also improves TabPFN on classification and regression benchmark suites. These results support both richer synthetic training challenges and a more flexible architecture as useful ways to improve tabular prediction without real-world pretraining data.
icml-2025-zero-shot-meta-learning-for-ta.tldr: APT learns from adversarial synthetic datasets and supports arbitrary class counts, matching leading small-table classification performance with subsecond average runtime.
